Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset of $\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let $a:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. The **convex hull** $\operatorname{conv}K$ is the set of finite convex combinations of points of $K$. A **phase generator** is a point $y\in K$ with declared energy $a(y)$. A **mixture** is a Borel probability measure $P$ on $K$. Its barycenter and mean energy are the coordinatewise Lebesgue integrals
$$\bar y(P):=\int_K y\,dP(y)\in\mathbb R^d,\qquad \bar a(P):=\int_K a(y)\,dP(y)\in\mathbb R.$$
These integrals are finite because each coordinate and $a$ are bounded on compact $K$. For prescribed mean $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$, the **mixture energy** is
$$a_{\rm mix}(x):=\inf\{\bar a(P):P\text{ is a Borel probability on }K,\ \bar y(P)=x\}.$$
The admissible set is nonempty since every finite convex combination of points of $K$ is the barycenter of a finite atomic probability. The definition does not assert that the infimum is attained; the theorem on this page gives a compact continuous sufficient condition.

Let S be Polish in the sense of [[def-polish-space]]. A **Borel probability law on S** is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(S)$ with total mass one. Here $\mathcal B(S)$ is [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] and probability measure means [[def-probability-measure]]. A compatible complete metric may be fixed for a construction; it is not additional data in the law. The empty space admits no such law, since its measure must be both zero and one.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim: Define $\Phi(y)=(y,a(y))\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$ and $G=\Phi(K)$. The map $\Phi$ is continuous. The set $G$ is bounded because $\Phi[K]$ is bounded on compact $K$; it is closed because from any convergent sequence $\Phi(y_n)$, [F3] gives a subsequence $y_{n_j}\to y\in K$, and continuity gives $\Phi(y_{n_j})\to\Phi(y)$. Thus [F3] makes $G$ compact. [A1, F3, algebra]

Any finite convex combination of more than $d+2$ points of $G\subset\mathbb R^{d+1}$ has an affine dependence: there are coefficients $c_i$, not all zero, with $\sum_i c_i=0$ and $\sum_i c_i g_i=0$. Both signs occur. If its positive weights are $\theta_i$, replacing them by $\theta_i-tc_i$, where $t=\min_{c_i>0}\theta_i/c_i$, preserves their sum and combination, keeps them nonnegative, and makes at least one zero. Repeating gives at most $d+2$ points. Pad shorter combinations by zero weights and repeat any fixed point of nonempty $G$. It follows that $\operatorname{conv}G$ is the continuous image of the compact finite-dimensional parameter set $G^{d+2}\times\Delta_{d+2}$, where $\Delta_{d+2}=\{\theta_i\ge0:\sum_i\theta_i=1\}$. This set is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F3]; the same sequential argument as in 1.1 shows its image is compact. [A1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

Fix $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$. Its fiber $F_x=\{r:(x,r)\in\operatorname{conv}G\}$ is nonempty, since each finite convex combination of generators gives such a point, and compact, since it is a closed section of compact $\operatorname{conv}G$. Therefore [F4] gives a minimum $r_x$. A convex-combination representation of $(x,r_x)$ by points $(y_i,a(y_i))$ defines a finite atomic Borel probability $P_x$ with barycenter $x$ and energy $r_x$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, step 2.1]

Conversely, for any Borel probability $P$ on $K$, the vector-valued map $\Phi$ is bounded and coordinatewise integrable by [F2]. Its integral is in $\operatorname{conv}G$: for each $\epsilon>0$, uniform continuity of $\Phi$ gives a finite Borel partition of $K$ whose pieces have image diameter at most $\epsilon$. Choose a point in each nonempty piece and weight it by that piece's $P$-mass. The resulting finite convex combination differs coordinatewise from $\int\Phi\,dP$ by at most $\epsilon$; as $\operatorname{conv}G$ is closed by step 2.1, the integral belongs to it. If $\bar y(P)=x$, then $(x,\bar a(P))\in\operatorname{conv}G$, so $\bar a(P)\ge r_x$. Together with step 3.1 this proves that the all-measure infimum equals $r_x$ and is attained by $P_x$. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1]

To prove lower semicontinuity, let $x_n\to x$ in $\operatorname{conv}K$ and pass to a subsequence along which $a_{\rm mix}(x_n)$ tends to its liminf. The values lie between $\min_K a$ and $\max_K a$, attained by [F4], so a further subsequence of $(x_n,a_{\rm mix}(x_n))$ converges. Each pair lies in the compact set $\operatorname{conv}G$ by step 4.1; its limit is therefore $(x,r)\in\operatorname{conv}G$. The minimum in the fiber at $x$ satisfies $a_{\rm mix}(x)\le r=\liminf_n a_{\rm mix}(x_n)$. [A1, F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1]

Combine minimizers $P_x$ and $P_z$ with weights $s$ and $1-s$, $0\le s\le1$. The combined finite measure has barycenter $sx+(1-s)z$ and energy $s a_{\rm mix}(x)+(1-s)a_{\rm mix}(z)$. By step 4.1, the minimum at the combined barycenter is no greater than this value. Hence $a_{\rm mix}$ is convex. [F1, step 3.1, step 4.1]

The support reduction in 2.1 first gives at most $d+2$ atoms. If an optimal representation has more than $d+1$ positive weights, the points $y_i\in\mathbb R^d$ have an affine dependence $\sum_i c_i y_i=0$, $\sum_i c_i=0$. For sufficiently small positive $t$, both weight lists $\theta_i\pm t c_i$ remain nonnegative and preserve the barycenter. If $\sum_i c_i a(y_i)\ne0$, one of these lists strictly lowers energy, contradicting optimality; hence this sum is zero. Increase $t$ in one sign to the first value at which a positive coefficient becomes zero. The new weights preserve barycenter and energy and still attain the minimum; iteration leaves at most $d+1$ positive weights. [A1, F1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

Finally, let $g$ be any convex function on $\operatorname{conv}K$ with $g(y)\le a(y)$ for $y\in K$. For the finite optimal measure from 4.1, finite Jensen (obtained by iterating the two-point convexity inequality) gives $g(x)\le\sum_i\theta_i g(y_i)\le\sum_i\theta_i a(y_i)=a_{\rm mix}(x)$. Since $a_{\rm mix}(y)\le a(y)$ for $y\in K$ by the point mass at $y$, it is itself such a convex minorant and dominates every other one. [F1, step 5.1, step 5.2, algebra] ∎

boundaries.evidence: Statement: The nonempty generator hypothesis is used to construct G and a fiber minimizer .
Statement: Zero energy values are allowed; bounded minima and the point-mass comparison cover them .
Statement: The single-generator case has a singleton fiber and a one-atom optimizer .
Statement: Affine dependence removes redundant or repeated support points without changing the optimum .
Statement: Every boundary point x of conv K has a nonempty compact fiber; does not require interiority.
Statement: The minimum is obtained from a compact nonempty fiber and represented by finitely many generators .

boundaries.reason: The statement is an attainment and maximality theorem, not an iff characterization.
The statement is an attainment and maximality theorem, not an iff characterization.

finite_checks.check: For K={0,1}, a(0)=0, a(1)=1, and prescribed mean x=1/2, the only feasible weights are 1/2,1/2; the minimum is 1/2 with two atoms.
finite_checks.evidence: Substitute into the finite barycenter and energy sums in steps 2.1 and 4.1.
